newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Aborted Czech tank sale to Algeria splits govt.
newsitem.headline: Aborted Czech tank sale to Algeria splits govt.

text.p: Two junior parties in the shaky Czech government quarrelled openly on Thursday over an aborted Defence Ministry plan to sell 100 Soviet-era tanks to Algeria.

In a late-night session on Wednesday, the government rejected Defence Minister Miloslav Vyborny's plan to sell the refurbished T-72 tanks to Algiers via private Czech arms trading firm Omnipol, a unit of Chemapol a.s..
Proceeds from the sale were intended to buy new Czech-made L-39 light fighter planes from Aero a.s..
A source familiar with the debate said the plan was scuttled by ministers who complained that the deal was drawn up behind the backs of the government.
They said it was not clear why the ministry could part with the tanks now when in March they were listed as necessary for the army's strategic planning.
The source said the decision had nothing to do with Algeria being the intended customer.
Vyborny said he had offered his resignation to President Vaclav Havel, but that Havel rejected it as "politically dangerous" an told Vyborny he still had Havel's trust.
"I'm not going to make any gesture just for prestige," he told a news conference after a hurried meeting of the three coalition party leaders.

The row widened the gulf between Vyborny's centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) and the right-wing Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA), leaving Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) split in between.
The government only has about 20 percent support in opinion polls after divisive debates on economic policy in the spring, and narrowly survived a confidence vote less than two months ago.
Vyborny sharply attacked the ODA and its leader Michal Zantovsky, calling the rejection of his plan "irrational".
Zantovsky, who holds no ministerial seat and has been a frequent critic of Vyborny, said the tank sale would not have been in the security interests of the country.
"The basic argument against (the sale) was that it was not motivated or dictated by the interest of the defence capabilities of this country," Zantovsky told reporters after the coalition meeting.

A presidential spokesman said Havel had asked Zantovsky to reconsider the tank sale but the news agency CTK said Zantovsky, Havel's former spokesman, rejected the appeal, saying the deal was a "closed issue".
Still unanswered was how much Klaus's senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS) was split on the tank sale.
The prime minister voted in favour of the sale, but votes from some of his party's eight ministers would have been required to kill the deal. Officials declined to say how each minister voted.
"I'm very sorry that the question of the sale of the tanks was transformed into a political fight," Klaus told reporters.
